page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: The RMS (root mean square) speed of a gas is
the square root of the mean of the squares of
the speeds of all the gas molecules.
steps.why: The name is the recipe read backwards: square every molecule's speed, take the mean of those squares, then take the root. That order matters — it is not the average speed.
common_mistakes: Defining it as the average of the speeds. Squaring comes first; RMS is slightly larger than the average speed.
Reversing the order of operations — the mean is taken of the SQUARES.
steps.memory_tip: Read the name right to left: Speed → Squared → Mean → Root.
steps.margin_note: The three operations in order — square, mean, root — are the marked content.

steps.label: The formula
steps.why: The first form is the definition written in symbols; the second comes from the kinetic gas equation and is the form every numerical uses, with T in kelvin and M the molar mass.
common_mistakes: Writing 2RT or 8RT/π under the root. Those belong to the most probable and average speeds.
steps.memory_tip: 3 goes with RMS — the biggest number under the root for the biggest of the three speeds.
steps.margin_note: Either form earns the mark; the √(3RT/M) form is the one to box.

insider_note: Asked five times across the years on record — a two-line answer with the definition in words plus √(3RT/M) has been full marks every time.
